The same structure exists in Queensland (Peaceful Assembly Act s 6), NSW (Summary Offences Act s 24) and Western Australia (Public Order in Streets Act) — four of nine jurisdictions regulate protest primarily through conditional immunity rather than prohibition.

entries.short_title: Public Order in Streets Act 1984, Criminal Investigation Act 2006 s 27, and the Criminal Code
entries.full_title: Public Order in Streets Act 1984 (WA), Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) s 27, and Criminal Code (WA)
key_provisions: There is no offence of holding a public meeting or procession without a permit; the permit's function is protective, supplying immunity from traffic and obstruction charges. Notice to the Commissioner of Police at least 4 days beforehand.

The Commissioner may refuse only on reasonable grounds to apprehend serious public disorder, property damage, excessive or prolonged obstruction, or a risk to safety. Section 8: review of a refusal to the State Administrative Tribunal.

Criminal Investigation Act 2006 s 27: police may order a person to move on for up to 24 hours; the statutory grounds and penalty for breach could not be confirmed and should be checked before publication.

Other offences commonly used against protesters: Criminal Code (WA) s 62 unlawful assembly (12 months or $12,000), s 65 riot (5–10 years), s 70A trespass (12 months or $12,000), s 74A disorderly behaviour ($6,000); Road Traffic Code 2000 (WA) r 201 obstructing pedestrians or vehicles ($100).
entries.commentary: This is the permit regime that the Public Order Legislation Amendment Bill 2026 (see the Anti-Protest Legislation category) would tighten, by empowering police to refuse a permit on hate-promotion grounds. Reading the two together shows what is actually being changed: not a prohibition, but the conditions on which protective immunity is granted, together with a new discretionary refusal power. Western Australia has enacted no dedicated anti-protest statute; until 2026 it relied entirely on the general Criminal Code offences above and move-on powers — which is why the WA anti-protest entries in this tracker are mostly Bills rather than Acts, and why the outcome of the 2026 Bills matters for the national picture.

entries.short_title: Police Offences Act 1935
entries.full_title: Police Offences Act 1935 (Tas)
key_provisions: The general public order statute, and since the 2022 repeal of the Workplaces (Protection from Protesters) Act 2014 the primary vehicle for protest offences in Tasmania.

Section 13: public annoyance, including unreasonable obstruction of a street — penalty raised from 3 to 10 penalty units in 2022. Section 14B: trespass, with the aggravated workplace-protection provisions inserted in 2022 (see the Anti-Protest Legislation category).
Sections 6C and 6D: Nazi symbol and gesture prohibitions, inserted in 2023 (see the Political Violence, Hate and Extremism category).
entries.commentary: Tasmania is the clearest illustration of the drafting shift this tracker documents: from a standalone, protest-specific statute (2014, struck down 2017) to protest-specific penalties embedded within a general public order Act (2022). The conduct reached is substantially similar; the constitutional exposure is not. Because the offences now sit inside a general statute, protest prosecutions in Tasmania are considerably harder to identify from the legislation alone — charge-level coding will be needed to separate them from ordinary trespass matters, a data-collection implication worth recording in the codebook.

entries.short_title: Human Rights Act 2004 and Public Assemblies Act 1959
entries.full_title: Human Rights Act 2004 (ACT) and Public Assemblies Act 1959 (ACT)
key_provisions: The ACT Human Rights Act expressly protects the right to peaceful assembly and freedom of association (s 15) and freedom of expression (s 16). No formal approval is required for protests or demonstrations in most public spaces.
Permission is required for protests in parliamentary precincts (Parliamentary Precincts Act 1988 (Cth)) and diplomatic areas, and to erect structures as part of a protest.
entries.commentary: The ACT's human rights framework provides stronger protections for protest than any other Australian jurisdiction, and it has enacted no anti-protest legislation of the kind seen in NSW, Queensland, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia. Commonwealth laws, including the Parliamentary Precincts Act, still impose restrictions on protest in the national capital. The ACT is the control case for this tracker: a jurisdiction with comparable protest activity and no securitising legislative response — any claim that the post-2019 wave was a necessary response to changed protest tactics has to account for it.

entries.short_title: Summary Offences Act 1923 and Police Administration Act 1978
entries.full_title: Summary Offences Act 1923 (NT) and Police Administration Act 1978 (NT)
key_provisions: Permit required to protest in a public place. Move-on powers: police may issue move-on directions, and failure to comply is a criminal offence; move-on orders do not apply to authorised public assemblies.

CORRECTION: the previous version of this tracker cited the 'Police Administration Act 2014 (NT)'. The principal Act is the Police Administration Act 1978 (NT); this entry's citation has been corrected accordingly.
entries.commentary: The Northern Territory has not introduced specific anti-protest legislation targeting environmental or political activism; the permit system and move-on powers are the primary regulatory tools. The NT's smaller population and different political dynamics have meant less legislative focus on protest securitisation than in the south-eastern states. Together with the ACT, the NT provides the comparison set for jurisdictions that did not legislate — as analytically necessary as the jurisdictions that did.

key_cases.outcome: Key operative provisions invalid in their operation on forestry land, 5:2 (Gordon and Edelman JJ dissenting) — the first invalidation of anti-protest legislation on implied freedom grounds.

key_cases.case_name: Clubb v Edwards; Preston v Avery
key_cases.provision_considered: Abortion clinic safe access zones (Vic and Tas)
key_cases.outcome: Legislation upheld — the principal authority for the proposition that content-neutral protest restrictions may be proportionate.

key_cases.case_name: Kvelde v State of New South Wales
key_cases.court_year: NSW Supreme Court, Walton J, 13 December 2023
key_cases.provision_considered: Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s 214A; Roads Regulation 2018 cl 48A(1)
key_cases.outcome: Section 214A(1)(c) and (d) invalid; (a) and (b), and cl 48A(1), valid. Walton J also criticised Summary Offences Act 1988 Part 4 for failing to accommodate spontaneous protest.

key_cases.case_name: Lees v State of New South Wales
key_cases.court_year: NSW Supreme Court, Mitchelmore J, 16 October 2025
key_cases.provision_considered: LEPRA s 200(5), inserted by the Crimes Amendment (Places of Worship) Act 2025
key_cases.outcome: Invalid. Failed at the necessity stage: an obvious and compelling alternative existed, limited to protests affecting persons accessing or leaving a place of worship.

key_cases.case_name: Jarrett v State of New South Wales
key_cases.provision_considered: Public Assembly Restriction Declaration scheme, Terrorism (Police Powers) Act 2002 (NSW) Pt 2 Div 3A
key_cases.outcome: Scheme invalid. 'Social cohesion' held not to be a constitutionally legitimate end in itself. Applied the test as restated in Ravbar (2025). Whether special leave to appeal to the High Court has been sought is unconfirmed.
Upheld 5:2 (Kirby and Hayne JJ dissenting) — the first constitutional test of the post-9/11 preventive architecture.

key_cases.case_name: Alexander v Minister for Home Affairs
key_cases.outcome: Invalid. Ministerial citizenship cessation for conduct is punitive and therefore exclusively judicial.

key_cases.case_name: Benbrika v Minister for Home Affairs
key_cases.outcome: Invalid. Punishment of criminal conduct is exclusively judicial even when severed from adjudication. Note: [2023] HCA 33, not [2023] HCA 25.

key_cases.case_name: Minister for Home Affairs v Benbrika
key_cases.outcome: Upheld. The majority found an evident non-punitive, protective purpose.

key_cases.court_year: Queensland Supreme Court, Applegarth J, 8 August 2020
key_cases.outcome: Ex parte interlocutory injunction restraining a planned Story Bridge sit-in. Rights acknowledged, limitation held justified. Not a final determination on the assembly scheme.

key_cases.provision_considered: Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (Vic) ss 15, 16, 32(1)
key_cases.outcome: Charges against 16 accused dismissed — the clearest Victorian example of Charter rights defeating protest charges. First instance only, not binding, and unreported.

key_cases.court_year: Victorian Supreme Court, Harris J, 12 December 2025
key_cases.provision_considered: Police use of OC foam at the 2019 IMARC protest
key_cases.outcome: Two OC foam deployments were batteries without lawful justification; the ss 322K, 322N and 462A defences failed. Damages $54,000, including $10,000 aggravated.

themes.title: Bipartisan support for anti-protest legislation
themes.summary: A notable feature of the post-2019 wave of anti-protest legislation is that it has been introduced by both Labor and Coalition governments. Queensland (2019), Victoria (2022), South Australia (2023), and NSW (2022, 2025) all enacted significant restrictions under governments of different political persuasions, suggesting broad bipartisan consensus on the securitisation of protest.

themes.title: Constitutional limits: the implied freedom of political communication
themes.summary: Several anti-protest laws have been wholly or partially struck down by courts on the basis that they impermissibly burden the implied freedom of political communication under the Commonwealth Constitution. Key cases include Brown v Tasmania [2017] HCA 43; Kvelde v State of New South Wales [2023] NSWSC 1560; and Lees v State of New South Wales [2025] NSWSC 1209.

themes.title: The terrorism–protest nexus
themes.summary: The use of counter-terrorism powers in the context of protest represents a significant expansion of the security state into the domain of civil liberties. NSW's Public Assembly Restriction Declarations (2025–2026) and Victoria's use of special police powers at protest events (2024–2025) illustrate how terrorism legislation has been deployed to manage and restrict protest activity.

themes.title: Escalating penalties
themes.summary: The period under review has seen a dramatic escalation in penalties for protest-related offences. South Australia's increase from a $750 fine to $50,000 (a 6,567% increase) is the most striking example, but similar patterns are evident across jurisdictions. The introduction of imprisonment as a penalty for obstruction-type offences, and provisions allowing cost-recovery from protesters, represents a shift from treating protest as a regulatory matter to treating it as serious criminal conduct.

themes.title: Environmental protest as the primary target
themes.summary: Much of the anti-protest legislation enacted between 2014 and 2023 was introduced in direct response to environmental and climate activism. Since 2024–2025, legislation has also targeted pro-Palestine protest activity, particularly in NSW. This suggests that the 'securitisation of protest' is not limited to any single issue but adapts to whichever form of dissent is most politically salient.
